facts.fact: Total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) is made up of toxic un-ionized ammonia (NH3) and much less toxic ammonium (NH4+).
The share of toxic NH3 goes up as pH and temperature rise. pH has the bigger effect.
Most test kits measure TAN, not NH3, so the NH3 fraction has to be calculated from pH and temperature.
Freshwater fish usually tolerate TAN below 1 mg/L. Saltwater fish usually tolerate TAN below 0.5 mg/L.
Un-ionized ammonia below 0.05 mg/L is generally not considered harmful. A calculated NH3 of 0.05 mg/L or more can damage gills.
About 2 mg/L of un-ionized ammonia is lethal to many fish.
Merck says a TAN of 1.0 is not a major concern in most home aquariums unless pH is above 8.5.
Nitrite above 0.1 mg/L is listed as toxic, especially in freshwater with little chloride.
Most nitrite kits report nitrite-nitrogen. Multiply the reading by 3.3 to get NO2.
Nitrite turns hemoglobin into methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen. Fish can suffocate even in water with plenty of oxygen. This is called 'brown blood disease'.
Nitrite crosses the gills into the blood and forms methemoglobin (met-hemocyanin in invertebrates), which cannot bind oxygen.
Low dissolved oxygen makes nitrite's effect on breathing worse.
Nitrite becomes more toxic as temperature rises. The sea bass LC50 fell from 274 mg/L at 17°C to 154 mg/L at 27°C.
Ammonia is more toxic at higher pH and in warmer water, and ammonia problems often come together with nitrite problems.
Estimated safe long-term nitrite-nitrogen levels are 0.5000–2.5000 mg/L for freshwater warmwater fish and invertebrates, and 0.0125–0.5000 mg/L for freshwater coldwater fish.
Ammonia poisoning causes lethargy, poor appetite or refusal to eat, darker coloration, and sometimes sudden mass deaths.
Acute ammonia toxicity can cause spinning, disorientation and convulsive swimming.
Under the microscope, ammonia-damaged gills show cell hyperplasia, enlarged chloride cells and fused lamellae.
Nitrite poisoning turns the gills chocolate-brown and the blood abnormally dark. The color change may only show once methemoglobin levels are high.
Fish with nitrite poisoning look for oxygen: they gather in well-oxygenated spots or gulp at the surface (piping).
Merck lists high nitrite as one cause of gulping at the surface, along with low oxygen and gill disease. Testing the water tells these causes apart.
Nitrite toxicity also causes gill lesions and swelling (edema) in skeletal muscle.
Ammonia builds up from overfeeding, a failed or dead biofilter, or ammonia or chloramine in the source water.
New tank syndrome: NH3 rises in the first 2–3 weeks and NO2 may rise later because the filter bacteria are not established yet.
Treating chloramine tap water with sodium thiosulfate releases ammonia, so repeated water changes can raise ammonia, especially when the biofilter is new or damaged.
Old tank syndrome comes from too few water changes. Organic acids lower pH (usually below 6) and use up alkalinity, while TAN can go above 20 mg/L.
Antimicrobials and other chemicals can damage the biofilter.

Common causes of an ammonia spike are uneaten food or dead fish, overfeeding, overstocking, rinsing filter media under the tap or replacing it with new media, and adding fish to a tank whose filter is not yet mature.
As soon as high NH3 is found, change at least 50% of the water.
Test the source water for ammonia and chloramine first, because a water change can add more ammonia.
If TAN is above 5 mg/L and pH is below 7, move the fish to a clean system with matching temperature and pH. Otherwise the ammonia can suddenly turn toxic when pH rises.
Stop feeding, or cut feeding sharply, until the problem is fixed.
Change 50–75% of the water with dechlorinated tap water of similar temperature and chemistry. This dilutes ammonia quickly, but the effect may not last.
Add aeration with air stones, a venturi, or filter outlets aimed at the surface, because ammonia irritates the gills.
When ammonia is found, also test nitrite, pH and temperature.
Fish with brown blood disease recover quickly once moved to water low in nitrite.
Salt (chloride) can stop deaths during a sudden nitrite spike in many freshwater fish because chloride competes with nitrite for uptake at the gills.
Many ponds and aquariums keep a residual salt level of 1–3 ppt (1 g/L = 1 ppt), which makes nitrite poisoning less likely.
Chloride at least 20 times the nitrite-nitrogen concentration should counteract nitrite toxicity in channel catfish and probably most freshwater species.
Channel catfish farmers usually keep chloride at 50–100 mg/L with sodium chloride to prevent brown blood disease.
Adding sodium chloride is described as not feasible in brackish or marine systems.
A Vietnamese hobbyist article says about 20 ppm chloride can prevent nitrite poisoning.
A Vietnamese hobbyist article gives 1–3 g of salt per litre for long-term soaking, and says to use plain salt, not iodized salt.
For old tank syndrome, Merck advises aggressive water changes plus an over-the-counter ammonia neutralizer, so the ammonia does not suddenly turn toxic as pH rises.
Zeolite filter media or an ammonia-neutralizing liquid can give short-term relief.
Seachem Prime binds ammonia, nitrite and nitrate into a non-toxic form that biofilter bacteria can still use. It does not remove them.
Prime's standard dose is 5 mL (1 capful) per 200 L. Each cap thread is about 1 mL.
Prime's binding lasts up to 48 hours. Redose every 24–48 hours, or every 24 hours if ammonia or nitrite keeps rising.
For nitrite emergencies, or when ammonia or nitrite is above 2 ppm, Seachem says up to 5 times the normal Prime dose may be used.
Seachem advises a half dose of Prime when water is above 30 °C and chlorine or ammonia levels are low.
A Vietnamese hobbyist article says tetras and elephantnose fish do not tolerate high-salt water.
Step 1: test ammonia and nitrite, and also pH and temperature.
Step 2: increase aeration.
Step 3: change 50–75% of the water with dechlorinated water of matching temperature.
Step 4: find and fix the cause, such as a dead fish, overfeeding, overstocking or a damaged filter.
Step 5: add an ammonia remover or neutralizer for short-term relief, and optionally a bacterial supplement.
Step 6: keep testing and doing partial water changes until levels are back to normal. Ammonia can rebound and nitrite problems can follow.
In a new tank, test TAN and nitrite every day and change water often until the biofilter matures. It usually takes about 6 weeks.
The biofilter is mature when TAN and nitrite peak and then fall, followed by a rise in nitrate.
Do not overstock or overfeed, especially in new tanks. Use commercial nitrifying bacteria, feed the bacteria with fish food or ammonium chloride before adding fish, or add fish slowly.
Keep alkalinity at least 100 mg/L in freshwater, and keep oxygen in the filter bed.
Use a dechlorinator made for chloramine, which also binds the ammonia it releases. Test both free and total chlorine.
Keep dissolved oxygen above 3 mg/L for warmwater species and above 5 mg/L for coldwater species. This also helps bacteria turn nitrite into nitrate.
Test nitrite regularly. Cheap test kits give fairly accurate results.
Rinsing filter media under tap water or replacing old media with new media can cause an ammonia spike.
Repeated water changes with chloramine-treated tap water and an ordinary dechlorinator can keep raising ammonia.
Reading a nitrite-nitrogen kit result as NO2 underestimates nitrite. The reading must be multiplied by 3.3.
Prime only binds ammonia and nitrite for up to 48 hours. If it is not redosed, they are released back into the water.
A Vietnamese aquaculture page describes nitrite poisoning as 'bệnh máu nâu' (brown blood disease) and says it is more common in freshwater than in brackish or marine water.
Vietnamese hobbyists use plain coarse salt ('muối hột') against nitrite. Iodized salt should not be used.
Because nitrite gets more toxic as temperature rises, the hot season raises the risk. LC50 values fall at higher temperatures, for example from 17°C to 27°C in sea bass.
Channel catfish are very sensitive to nitrite. Centrarchids (bass and bluegill) are fairly resistant.
Marine fish are not fully protected: red drum have developed brown blood disease from nitrite.
Coldwater species are much more sensitive to nitrite. Rainbow trout LC50s (0.24–11.0 mg/L) are four or more times lower than those of channel catfish (7.1–44.0 mg/L).
Freshwater prawns are highly sensitive to nitrite, with a 96-h LC50 of 8.6 mg/L nitrite-nitrogen.
Seachem says it does not fully understand how Prime detoxifies nitrite and nitrate, and that customer reports support the effect.
